reviewContext.abstract: family-law-benchmark An open benchmark for family law AI — 109 long-horizon tasks across 16 domains. Inspired by Harvey LAB, built as a standalone project. # Family Law Benchmark **The open benchmark for family law AI — the measuring stick for the highest-volume, most-underserved area of legal practice.** *Inspired by Harvey's LAB. Built as a standalone project, not a contribution to it.* Prepared by Ben Craig — August 2026 Status: Draft for review (rubrics pending validation by a licensed family law attorney) --- ## 1. What this is This is a standalone benchmark for evaluating AI agents on real family law work — divorce, custody, child support, domestic violence, paternity, adoption, and the rest of the domestic-relations docket. It is **not** a contribution to Harvey's LAB. It is a separate project, inspired by LAB's methodology, built to own the measuring stick for a practice area LAB does not cover. LAB (Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark) is the leading open benchmark for legal AI: 1,250+ tasks across 24 practice areas, graded on tens of thousands of lawyer-written rubric criteria. But all 24 of those practice areas are corporate — mergers, banking, private equity, tax, real estate, intellectual property. BigLaw work. Family law is absent. This project fills that gap — not by asking to join LAB, but by building the family law counterpart to it, openly and independently. ## 2. Why family law Family law is the single largest category of civil filings in nearly every US jurisdiction. It dwarfs the corporate work LAB covers in raw case count. And it is the most underserved: - **Highest volume.** Domestic relations is the largest category of civil filings in nearly every US jurisdiction. - **Highest pro se rate.** Between 70% and 80% of family law cases involve at least one self-represented party. The people in this system need automated help the most and have the least access to it. - **No one owns the niche.** The legal AI field is focused on BigLaw. Family law — high volume, low dollars per case — is not BigLaw's moneymaker, so it has been left behind. That is exactly why it is the biggest opening. - **State-specificity is a hard test.** Child support formulas, property-division regimes, and best-interest factors differ by state. A benchmark here directly measures whether an agent applies the *correct* jurisdiction's law rather than pattern-matching generic legal language. - **Recurring, not one-off.** Family cases generate a stream of follow-on matters — modifications, enforcement, contempt, relocation — that test an agent's ability to track a matter over time. ## 3. Design principles Each task follows the same philosophy as LAB: long-horizon, grounded in real documents, producing a concrete deliverable, graded against expert-written rubric criteria. 1. **Long-horizon.** No task is a single question. Each requires reading documents, identifying issues, applying the governing law, and producing a filing or analysis. 2. **Document-grounded.** Every task supplies realistic input documents (petitions, income and expense declarations, asset/debt schedules, prior orders, correspondence). The agent must work from these, not from general knowledge. 3. **Jurisdiction-specified.** Each task names a state. A correct answer requires applying that state's law. This is the core competency being measured. 4. **Rubric-graded.** Each task carries pass/fail rubric criteria. Two scores are reported, matching LAB: criterion pass rate (share of criteria met) and all-pass rate (share of tasks where every criterion passes). 5. **No-citation-hallucination.** Rubrics explicitly reward the agent for citing only authorities present in the supplied materials and penalize invented citations. 6. **Synthetic facts only.** All people, names, dates, and documents are fictional. No real client material, no real parties, no real case facts. --- ## 4. Practice areas covered | Domain | Tasks | |---|---| | Dissolution, Annulment & Legal Separation | 10 | | Child Custody, Visitation & Relocation | 22 | | Child Support & Enforcement | 13 | | Spousal Support (Alimony) | 5 | | Property Division & Financial | 15 | | Domestic Violence & Protective Orders | 5 | | Paternity, Parentage & Assisted Reproduction | 9 | | Adoption | 6 | | Guardianship & Conservatorship | 4 | | Juvenile Dependency (CPS) | 5 | | Name Change | 3 | | Military & Interstate Family Law | 3 | | Emancipation | 1 | | Domestic Partnership & Civil Union | 2 | | Mediation & Alternative Dispute Resolution | 3 | | Appeals & Post-Judgment | 3 | --- ## 5. The tasks ### Dissolution, Annulment & Legal Separation ### Task 1 — Petition for Dissolution of Marriage **Jurisdiction:** Hawaii (First Circuit) **Work type:** draft **Scenario:** A party with one minor child seeks a no-fault dissolution after a one-year separation. The client's intake form lists the marriage date, separation date, child's name/age, and a request for shared custody and guideline child support. **Input documents:** Client intake form; child's birth certificate; a prior temporary restraining order that was later dismissed. **Deliverable:** A completed petition for dissolution. **Rubric criteria (pass/fail):** - Correctly identifies Hawaii as a no-fault state and states the proper ground (irretrievable breakdown), not a fault ground. - Accurately recites the statutory residency/domicile requirement (HRS 580-1: six months). - Correctly lists the minor child and requests legal/physical custody as a distinct issue from property division. - Does not assert any fact not present in the intake form or supplied documents. - References the dismissed TRO accurately (dismissed, not "pending" or "active") — no fabrication of the DV history. - Produces a document in a captioned, fileable format (parties, case caption, signature block). ### Task 2 — Default / Uncontested Divorce (Pro Se) **Jurisdiction:** Hawaii (First Circuit) **Work type:** draft **Scenario:** A self-represented party with no minor children and no si

evidence.snippet: In this work, we present a systematic compute-platform benchmark of neural 3D reconstruction methods, evaluating NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting training and rendering on GPU-enabled computing devices ranging from single-board computers to server-class nodes, and place Meta's SAM3D single-image reconstruction on the same axes to quantify its latency and fidelity gap relative to per-scene optimization.
reasonCodes: benchmark release stated in one sentence

reviewContext.abstract: Autonomous robots performing laboratory tasks depend on 3D reconstruction pipelines that can turn raw camera streams into actionable object representations within the latency budget of a physical control loop. Neural 3D reconstruction methods have demonstrated high-quality view synthesis, but their real-time viability across the compute platforms on which laboratory robots actually run remains poorly characterized. In this work, we present a systematic compute-platform benchmark of neural 3D reconstruction methods, evaluating NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting training and rendering on GPU-enabled computing devices ranging from single-board computers to server-class nodes, and place Meta's SAM3D single-image reconstruction on the same axes to quantify its latency and fidelity gap relative to per-scene optimization. Our results show that Gaussian Splatting yields higher rendering quality than NeRF at greater GPU cost, and that onboard compute is insufficient for full per-scene optimization at interactive rates. Our preliminary assessment on SAM3D indicates that it delivers plausible object geometry within seconds, but with detail mismatches that can compromise downstream manipulation. Together, these findings motivate tiered pipelines in which lightweight feed-forward reconstruction sustains the real-time perception-and-tracking loop for laboratory robots, while heavier neural reconstruction is scheduled selectively on suitable compute.

reviewContext.abstract: clinical-ml-benchmark-breast-cancer Benchmark de Machine Learning para classificação de tumores benignos e malignos com modelos clássicos, seleção de variáveis e interpretabilidade. machine-learning matplotlib pandas python sckit-learn # Onco ML Benchmark Benchmark de Machine Learning para classificação de tumores benignos e malignos usando modelos clássicos, seleção de variáveis e interpretabilidade. ## Sobre o projeto A proposta é comparar diferentes algoritmos clássicos de Machine Learning para classificar tumores como benignos ou malignos, utilizando o dataset público Breast Cancer Wisconsin Diagnostic Dataset, disponível diretamente na biblioteca `scikit-learn`. O foco do projeto é mostrar um fluxo completo de Machine Learning, passando por análise exploratória, treinamento de modelos, avaliação, validação cruzada, seleção de variáveis e interpretabilidade. ## Objetivo O principal objetivo deste projeto é responder à seguinte pergunta: > É possível classificar tumores benignos e malignos utilizando modelos clássicos de Machine Learning de forma bem avaliada, interpretável e tecnicamente organizada? Para isso, o projeto busca demonstrar: * análise exploratória dos dados; * entendimento da variável alvo; * comparação entre modelos clássicos de Machine Learning; * uso de métricas adequadas para problemas médicos; * validação cruzada para avaliação mais robusta; * seleção de variáveis relevantes; * análise de interpretabilidade do modelo; * investigação de falsos negativos. ## Dataset O dataset utilizado foi o **Breast Cancer Wisconsin Diagnostic Dataset**, disponível no `scikit-learn`. Ele pode ser carregado com: ```python from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer ``` O dataset possui: * 569 registros; * 30 variáveis preditoras numéricas; * 1 variável alvo binária; * classes relacionadas a tumores benignos e malignos. No dataset original: ```text 0 = malignant 1 = benign ``` Para facilitar a interpretação clínica das métricas, o target foi ajustado no projeto para: ```text 0 = benigno 1 = maligno ``` Com esse ajuste, métricas como `precision`, `recall` e `F1-score` passam a considerar a classe maligna como classe positiva. ## Por que ajustar o target? Em problemas médicos, a interpretação das métricas precisa ser feita com cuidado. Neste projeto, o erro mais crítico é o **falso negativo**, que ocorre quando: ```text O tumor é maligno, mas o modelo classifica como benigno. ``` Por isso, o target foi ajustado para que a classe positiva seja `maligno`. Assim, o `recall` passa a representar a capacidade do modelo de identificar corretamente os tumores malignos. ## Tecnologias utilizadas O projeto foi desenvolvido em Python, utilizando principalmente: * Pandas; * NumPy; * Matplotlib; * Seaborn; * Scikit-learn; * SHAP. ## Técnicas aplicadas Durante o projeto foram aplicadas as seguintes técnicas: * Análise Exploratória de Dados; * tratamento e entendimento da variável alvo; * separação entre treino e teste; * divisão estratificada dos dados; * padronização com `StandardScaler`; * pipelines de Machine Learning; * treinamento de modelos supervisionados; * avaliação com múltiplas métricas; * validação cruzada estratificada; * seleção de variáveis; * importância por permutação; * análise de falsos negativos; * interpretabilidade com SHAP. ## Modelos avaliados Foram comparados os seguintes modelos clássicos de Machine Learning: * Logistic Regression; * K-Nearest Neighbors; * Support Vector Machine; * Decision Tree; * Random Forest; * Gradient Boosting. A ideia foi avaliar diferentes tipos de algoritmos: * modelos lineares; * modelos baseados em distância; * modelos baseados em margem; * árvores de decisão; * ensembles. ## Métricas utilizadas Os modelos foram avaliados com as seguintes métricas: * Accuracy; * Precision; * Recall; * F1-score; * ROC AUC; * Matriz de Confusão; * Curva ROC. Embora a acurácia seja uma métrica importante, ela não foi analisada de forma isolada. Como este projeto envolve classificação médica, o **recall da classe maligna** recebeu atenção especial, pois falsos negativos representam tumores malignos classificados incorretamente como benignos. ## Estrutura do projeto ```text onco-ml-benchmark/ │ ├── README.md │ └── notebooks/ ├── 01_eda_breast_cancer.ipynb ├── 02_model_training_and_baseline.ipynb ├── 03_cross_validation_and_model_selection.ipynb ├── 04_feature_selection.ipynb └── 05_model_interpretability.ipynb ``` ## Notebooks ### 01 - Análise Exploratória de Dados Neste notebook foi feita a primeira análise do dataset. Foram avaliados: * dimensões do dataset; * quantidade de variáveis; * tipos de dados; * distribuição das classes; * ausência de valores nulos; * estatísticas descritivas; * grupos de variáveis; * correlação com o target; * variáveis mais associadas ao diagnóstico. A análise mostrou que o dataset possui 569 registros, 30 variáveis preditoras numéricas e uma variável alvo binária. Também foi observado que as variáveis mais associadas ao diagnóstico estão relacionadas principalmente a: * pontos côncavos; * perímetro; * raio; * área; * concavidade; * compacidade. Essas variáveis representam características relacionadas à forma, tamanho e irregularidade das células analisadas. ### 02 - Treinamento e Baseline de Modelos Neste notebook foram treinados os primeiros modelos baseline. Foram aplicados: * `train_test_split`; * divisão estratificada; * `Pipeline`; * `StandardScaler`; * treinamento de múltiplos modelos; * avaliação com métricas de classificação. O objetivo foi criar uma primeira comparação entre diferentes algoritmos e entender o desempenho inicial de cada modelo. ### 03 - Validação Cruzada e Seleção de Modelo Neste notebook foi aplicada validação cruzada estratificada. A validação cruzada foi utilizada para reduzir a dependência de uma única divisão entre treino e teste. reviewContext.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) promises to accelerate biological research by automating computational analyses. Yet the ability of AI agents to carry out computational biology at the scale of complete research studies has not been systematically evaluated. Here we introduce BixBench3, a benchmark that measures the capacity of AI agents to process raw biological data through to scientific results. We designed BixBench3 tasks to mirror the delegation of work from a scientist to an agent: the scientist chooses the research question and high-level methods, then delegates implementation of all analyses to the agent. In each task, an agent receives a research objective, methodological guidance, and raw data derived from a published scientific study, and must execute a sequence of analyses to achieve the research objective. The data artifacts resulting from these analyses - such as peak call matrices or differential expression tables - are programmatically graded against the corresponding artifacts generated and reported in the original study. Across 20 BixBench3 tasks encompassing the generation of 138 unique artifacts, we find that 13 frontier models achieve scores ranging from 0.00 for Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite to 0.48 for GPT 5.6 Sol. Agents perform worse on tasks with larger raw datasets (0.36 on tasks with <100 GB versus 0.10 on tasks with >100 GB) and on analyses requiring more sequential steps (0.36 at 1-2 steps vs 0.24 at 3+). On average, agents use 6.8 hours, 102 million tokens, and $43 to complete each task, with the longest attempts consuming 24 hours, 1.07 billion tokens, and $525. Notably, the highest-scoring agents used fewer tokens and were cheaper than less performant options. These results reveal that LLMs vary substantially in their ability to (1) execute multiple sequential analysis steps coherently, (2) manage large quantities of raw data, and (3) work across scientific domains.

reviewContext.abstract: bench-your-bugs Build a private benchmark from the bugs you already fixed, and find out whether AI review actually catches them. Local, your code, your answer key. benchmark claude-code code-review developer-tools evals llm llm-evaluation qa regression-testing testing # Your own bug benchmark [![selftests](https://github.com/vladislav-andriushchenko/bench-your-bugs/actions/workflows/selftests.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/vladislav-andriushchenko/bench-your-bugs/actions/workflows/selftests.yml) **Build a private benchmark out of the bugs you have already fixed, and find out whether AI review actually catches them.** It runs on your machine, on your code, against your own answer key. A Claude Code subscription and `bash` are all it needs — no API key, no second provider, no orchestration. ```bash ./bench.sh from-commit a1b2c3d --repo ~/my-project # a bug you fixed becomes a test case ./bench.sh run # three passes, one table ``` The first command checks out the file as it was *before* your fix, keeps the fix itself where the model cannot see it, and turns the diff into the expected answer. Twenty seconds per bug. Fix ten bugs over a month and you own a benchmark nobody else has. ## Why a private benchmark beats a public score Public leaderboards answer a question you do not have. This one answers three you do. **Your bugs are not in anyone's training data.** Public benchmarks leak into training sets and stop measuring anything. Yesterday's commit in your repository cannot. **Your bug classes are not the average bug class.** If your pain is idempotency, or timezone arithmetic, or one API contract that everyone gets wrong, no general benchmark will tell you whether a model catches *that*. **It answers "better or worse than last week".** You edit an instruction file, rewrite a skill, or a new model version ships. Rerun the same cases. Today that question gets answered by feel; this turns it into a number. The two benches in this repository are worked examples of the same method, not the product: one on planted bugs in code review, one on search tools. The machinery is what transfers. ## See it work in five seconds The search bench has every raw tool answer committed, so scoring re-runs with nothing installed beyond `bash` and `grep`: ```bash git clone https://github.com/vladislav-andriushchenko/bench-your-bugs cd bench-your-bugs/search ./selftest.sh # the scorer, checked against fake answers with known verdicts ./score.sh # rescores the committed answers and reproduces the published table ``` No keys, no network, no model calls. If those two commands pass, the whole method just demonstrated itself on your machine. ## The one thing that cannot be automated The answer key. A model that plants a bug and then writes its own expected answer is measuring itself, and it will hand you a clean green number that means nothing. So the answer key is not invented, it is harvested. A commit that fixed a bug is ground truth verified by reality: it knows what was wrong and where. `from-commit` reads it and builds the case. What stays manual is picking a commit that genuinely fixed a bug, and glancing at the generated pattern. Seconds, not hours — but not zero, and it cannot be zero. One bias to keep in mind: only bugs that were **found and fixed** can enter the corpus. The ones that shipped and were never noticed are exactly the ones you would most want to catch, and they are not here. ## The method, in three rules **1. Ground truth is fixed before the run, and never comes from the tools being compared.** In the search bench every expected answer is recorded in [`search/ORACLE.md`](search/ORACLE.md) before any tool runs, and each one is verified against a primary source using a tool that does not take part in the comparison. Score the tools against each other and you measure agreement, not correctness. **2. There is no LLM judge.** Scoring is `grep` over the tool's raw output against patterns committed alongside the ground truth. A judge model adds its own errors and its own bill, and a marker either appears in the text or it does not. **3. The scorer has its own selftest.** `./selftest.sh` in both benches runs the scorer against hand-written fake answers with known verdicts. reviewContext.abstract: ai-agent-intern-benchmark Rubric、Verifier、增量 Skill 与真实 A/B 实验记录 # 机房设备停机检修判定：评分器与增量 Skill 本仓库把一个依赖规范、巡检数据和空白交付模板的 Agent 任务补齐为可评分、可复现的最小 Benchmark。新增内容为 `rubric.md`、`verifier/verify.py`、`skill/SKILL.md` 与评分器测试；`材料/`、`任务书.md`、`gold/` 均保持只读、未改动。 ## 难点判断 难点不在 CSV 写入，而在把多个条款按正确优先级组合：缺失的设备级限值不是“无数据即跳过”，而要沿规范规定的回退路径取机柜级限值；告警条件与温度条件是并列触发；排除状态又会覆盖表面上的温度触发；有显式设备限值时不能误用机柜默认值。专业人员最容易卡在“逐列看数值”到“按条款建立决策顺序”的转换，以及把最终结论、触发条款和可审计数值同时落入既有模板。Rubric 因而将结果、条款、数值证据、说明文档分别评分，并把需要理解自然语言因果关系的部分留给人工或模型。 ## 评分设计 - 总分：100 分。 - 程序化小计：80 分，由 `verifier/verify.py` 完全判定。 - 语义小计：20 分，由人工或模型依照 `rubric.md` 判定；程序输出明确标为“待人工/模型判定”。 - Verifier 不读取提交目录之外的 Gold，也不依赖第三方库；期望值固化在程序中，避免参赛提交替换 Gold 影响评分。 - 证据字段采用“关键事实分组匹配”，容忍空格、全半角符号、`℃/摄氏度`、`>=/≥/不少于` 等表述差异；结论与条款因任务书限定了枚举值，按规范化后的精确值判定。 ## 运行方式 在 `任务包/` 目录执行： ```bash python3 verifier/verify.py gold python3 verifier/verify.py python3 -m unittest discover -s verifier/tests -v ``` 完整 Agent 对照实验需配置 Anthropic 兼容端点，并确保 Docker 可用： ```bash export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL= export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN= bash run.sh no_skill bash run.sh with_skill ``` `run.sh` 会分别生成 `runs/no_skill/` 与 `runs/with_skill/`，并自动调用 Verifier。两组统一授权 `Bash / Read / Grep / Glob / Write / Edit`，避免工具权限成为实验混杂变量。本次实际使用 Docker 镜像 `exam-task:local`、DeepSeek Anthropic 兼容端点和 `deepseek-v4-flash`，每组独立运行 5 次（共 10 次），记录位于 `runs/no_skill_01` 至 `runs/no_skill_05`、`runs/with_skill_01` 至 `runs/with_skill_05`。任务只有 4 个对象和 4 类关键规则，5 次/组足以观察本固定样例中解释遗漏是否重复出现、以及端到端交付是否稳定；但它不是模型总体成功率的统计估计，不能外推到其他任务。结果同时报告每次总分、逐条缺口、满分率和失败原因，而非只给平均分。 ## 已执行结果 ### Gold 自测 命令：`python verifier/verify.py gold` - 程序化得分：80 / 80。 - 语义部分：20 分明确标记为“待人工/模型判定”，未被程序自动计分。 - 当前自动得分：80 / 100；若 Gold 的语义项按 rubric 评审，预期完整总分为 100 / 100。 - 逐条程序化结果：P01–P10 全部通过。 ### Verifier 测试 测试覆盖 Gold 满分、缺文件、重复设备/缺行、非法判定、错误条款、只有空泛说明、跨设备事实泄漏、常见等价符号及较长但可审计的等价措辞。共 12 项，全部通过；原始输出记录在 `runs/verifier-tests.txt`。这组数据用于证明评分器的确定性与容错边界，不冒充 Agent A/B 实验。 ### Skill Gap Skill 定位为**增量型**：没有 Skill，Agent 仍可通过仔细阅读材料完成任务；Skill 只提供通用的规范驱动判定流程、例外优先级、缺失值回退、证据链和交付自检方法，不写入本任务的设备编号、条款号、温度、告警阈值或标准答案。 语义分由人工按 `rubric.md` 的 S01–S05 逐项复核；事实正确但因果链缺少“显式值优先/不回退”等环节时给半分。逐次结果如下，详细程序化分项见每个目录的 `_score.txt`，模型原始输出见 `_transcript.txt`，语义分项见 `runs/experiment-summary.csv`。 | 组别 | 运行 | 程序化 /80 | 语义 /20 | 总分 /100 | 关键差异或失败 | |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---| | 无 Skill | 01 | 80 | 20 | 100 | 全部通过 | | 无 Skill | 02 | 80 | 20 | 100 | 全部通过 | | 无 Skill | 03 | 76 | 18 | 94 | P10、S04：缺少显式值优先/不使用默认值说明 | | 无 Skill | 04 | 76 | 18 | 94 | P10、S04：只比较 78 与 75，未解释为何不用机柜默认值 | | 无 Skill | 05 | 80 | 20 | 100 | 全部通过 | | 使用 Skill | 01 | 80 | 20 | 100 | 全部通过 | | 使用 Skill | 02 | 80 | 20 | 100 | 全部通过 | | 使用 Skill | 03 | 80 | 20 | 100 | 全部通过 | | 使用 Skill | 04 | 80 | 20 | 100 | 全部通过 | | 使用 Skill | 05 | 80 | 20 | 100 | 全部通过 | 无 Skill 的程序化均分为 **78.4/80**、语义均分 **19.2/20**、总分均值 **97.6/100**，满分率 **3/5**；使用 Skill 的程序化均分为 **80/80**、语义均分 **20/20**、总分均值 **100/100**，满分率 **5/5**。两组中位数均为 100，完整交付率均为 5/5。Gap（使用 Skill − 无 Skill）为：程序化 **+1.6**、语义 **+0.8**、总分 **+2.4**。差异集中在 P10/S04：无 Skill 有两次虽然算对 78 > 75，却没有说明设备行已有显式限值时不启用机柜级回退值；使用 Skill 五次均把该优先关系写清。结论是：**在统一工具权限的本固定任务上，Skill 带来小幅但稳定的可审计性增益，并把满分率从 3/5 提高到 5/5；样本量和任务范围仍不足以支持广泛泛化。** 权限修正前的第一轮 5+5 作为 pilot 完整保留在 `runs/pilot_without_edit/`。该轮 `with_skill_03` 曾因运行器不允许 `Edit` 而未落盘，导致原始 Gap 为 −15.2；它被明确标记为工具权限混杂，不纳入上述主要效果结论，也没有被删除或覆盖。 Skill 中没有任务特定的具体数值、设备名称、条款号或阈值（即具体项为“无”），因此不存在答案泄漏。Skill 中的 `## When to use`、`## How to use` 是结构标题；“一行一个对象”等描述是通用数据处理原则，不对应 Gold 的具体答案。 ## A. 哪些判分点最可能误判正确提交，如何处理 P07–P10 最可能误判已经做对但措辞不同的提交，因为它们从自由文本中提取关键事实。处理方式是把每项拆成若干事实组，并为单位、比较符号、中文同义表达、长短句和数字格式设置候选模式；不要求复刻 Gold 原句，也不比较整段文本。两轮真实实验先后发现“与温度无关”“独立于温度”“数据行显式限值”“非空、无需回退”“80 但本行按 75”和较长数值比较等正确表达会被漏判，据此补充模式并新增回归测试；设备说明按每次设备编号出现形成局部块，既接受前后多次提及，又防止其他设备关键词串分。仍无法可靠程序化判断的因果链和规则优先级放入 S01–S05。P02 可能拒绝带汇总行的提交，但任务书明确要求每台设备一行，因此严格执行交付契约。 ## B. 已知但未解决的问题 Verifier 不能真正理解自然语言，关键词齐全但逻辑相反的证据文本仍可能通过 P07–P10；这由 20 分语义项补充检查。它只接受 CSV，不自动修复 Excel 方言、损坏编码或完全不同的表头。实验仍只有单一模型、单一任务、每组 5 次，不能估计普遍成功率；两组也没有可控的相同随机种子，因此运行编号只是重复序号，不是一一配对样本。语义分目前由人工依据 rubric 判定，仍可能带来评审者差异。权限修正前 pilot 暴露的 `Edit` 混杂已通过两组统一授权并完整重跑解决，但后续仍应预注册实验配置、增加任务集合与重复次数，并对语义裁判做盲化和一致性校准。 ## 文件说明 ```text rubric.md 100 分评分表（80 程序化 + 20 语义） verifier/verify.py 标准库实现的命令行评分器 verifier/tests/test_verify.py 评分器回归测试 skill/SKILL.md 增量型、无答案泄漏的通用工作方法 runs/gold-selftest.txt Gold 自测原始输出 runs/verifier-tests.txt 单元测试原始输出 runs/experiment-summary.csv 10 次实验的程序化、语义及总分明细 runs/*_01 ... *_05/ 两组逐次产物、原始转录和程序化评分 runs/pilot_without_edit/ 权限修正前的 5+5 pilot 与旧汇总（保留审计轨迹） ```

reviewContext.abstract: agent-layer-benchmark Frozen single-session benchmark comparing two agent-facing operational layers over the same nf-core pipelines # Operating nf-core pipelines through an agent: ClawBio and nf-claw A frozen, single-session benchmark comparing two agent-facing operational layers over the same `nf-core` pipelines. It measures the layer that surrounds the pipelines, never the scientific quality of the pipelines themselves, which is identical in both arms by construction. ## Experimental question > Which architecture allows a single agent task to discover, configure, validate, recover > and reproduce the same pipelines, on the same host, with less friction and stronger > observable guarantees? The analysis is descriptive. There is no composite score, no ranking and no confidence interval: the case bank is fixed and exhausted, and the experimental unit is one agent session, so `n = 1`. ## Frozen substrate | Architecture | Commit | |---|---| | ClawBio | `794dd1f5aacc1af308694c9b2f7966d0e396916e` | | nf-claw | `fbfd100798bd7959120f2db04d07de0a0c04ef72` | | Pipeline | Version | Upstream commit | |---|---|---| | `nf-core/scrnaseq` | 4.1.0 | `f7bf36d7c7e4bddc5302c3facd8d19ca83e22226` | | `nf-core/rnaseq` | 3.26.0 | `e7ca46272c8f9d5ceee3f71759f4ba551d3217a4` | | `nf-core/sarek` | 3.8.1 | `4bd2948f98c5bf7b785c91cf6708fffccab25467` | Both copies are cloned outside the original repositories, installed in two virtual environments with the same Python version, stripped of bytecode and held read-only for the whole run. ## The six axes | Axis | What it measures | Units | Deterministic | |---|---|---:|---| | B1 | architectural surface of the repository | 2 | yes | | B2 | discovery and first valid check | 6 | no | | B3 | documentary support for 36 decisions | 72 | no | | B4 | fault detection and recovery | 30 | no | | B5 | real execution and native-package auditability | 6 | no | | B6 | operational context cost, in tokens | 2 | yes | Mandatory order: `B2 → prewarm → prewarm closure → B1 → B6 → B3 → B4 → B5 → scoring`. B2 comes first because it measures the first exposure to the operational documentation; B1 follows the prewarm because its import timings are only comparable with the engine and images already warm. ## Results Run `20260826T055349Z-49a99444`, status `VALIDATED`, 118 of 118 units, scoring reproduced byte-identically in two independent passes. B6 separates the two architectures most clearly, and it is the one axis that involves no agent at all: operating a pipeline through ClawBio requires 2.06x to 2.22x the minimum context of nf-claw, and 1.87x to 2.20x the full operational documentation. The direction holds across all three pipelines. Every counted file is re-verified by hash against the frozen substrate, so the figure is reproducible from the substrate alone. B4 recovery favours ClawBio, 15 of 15 against 10 of 15. Detection sits at the ceiling in both arms, 12 of 12, with zero unsafe acceptances in either. B3 splits. The rejection half is a validity control at ceiling: 18 of 18 correct rejections and zero unsafe acceptances in both arms. On the acceptance half nf-claw is ahead, with 17 of 18 valid commands against 14 and 35 of 36 decisions correct against 32. B5 does not separate them: 46 of 54 criteria are met, 23 by each architecture. Seven of the eight misses are shared. Five fall on rerun instructions that name their original output directory, and two on the scrnaseq pair, where neither architecture records the identity of the container images that executed the pipeline. The remaining miss is ClawBio's sarek package, which does not state the upstream pipeline identity. Full figures and interpretation in [`results/`](results/). ## What the study does not support - That one architecture documents provenance better than the other. B5 ends level, 23 criteria each. - That any of these differences would hold for another model, host or case bank. The experimental unit is one session, so `n = 1`, and the case bank is fixed and exhausted rather than sampled. - That the differences are attributable to architecture alone. The three common versions are ClawBio's defaults, while nf-claw's frozen commit pins two of them at other versions. The protocol declares that asymmetry and the results preserve it. - Demonstrated equivalence from the axes at ceiling: a ceiling only shows the task fell below the difficulty threshold of both. - Any claim about the scientific quality of the pipelines, which is identical in both arms by construction. ## Repository layout ``` benchmark/ protocol, control-plane scripts and test suite protocol/BENCHMARK_PROTOCOL.md is the sealed document of record, SHA-256 6c5d524b5f055123..., bound to every manifest in results/ operator/ control scripts and the staged protocol views diagrams/ Mermaid diagrams of the design and the results results/ normalised results, manifests, seals, provenance packages and the requests delivered during the run translations/ English reading copies derived from the record, never replacing it verify.py re-derives the chain of custody from this repository alone ``` The six native provenance packages travel inside the evidence, each file hashed, so B5 can be re-audited without access to the original host. ## Reproducing The benchmark runs on a dedicated Linux host with at least 16 vCPU, 32 GiB of RAM and 500 GB of local SSD, with Docker and Nextflow 25.10.4. Start from [`benchmark/START_HERE.md`](benchmark/START_HERE.md). Every measured command passes through a registrar that refuses malformed or out-of-order invocations before execution, so a mistake costs nothing rather than a single-shot measurement. Scoring reads all inputs twice independently and requires identical bytes. ## How the run was executed The benchmark runs on a dedicated Linux host. The operator works from a local control post and never executes any part of the benchmark locally: every measured command runs on the host, inside the frozen bundle at `BENCH_ROOT`. ### Two machines, one role

reviewContext.abstract: Code-switching is pervasive in bilingual African conversation, yet most ASR systems assume monolingual input and are evaluated on curated monolingual benchmarks. We present AfriSwitch, a 61.36-hour human-transcribed benchmark of in-the-wild code-switched speech spanning 16 African languages and language varieties, released with switch-level English span tags, perutterance Code-Mixing Index (CMI), and switch-point counts. Corpus statistics show that mixing behaviour varies widely across African languages along two largely independent axes: how often speakers alternate, and how balanced the mixture is. No single scalar captures how code-switched a language is. Benchmarking five open and commercial multilingual ASR systems zero-shot yields word error rates far above published monolingual figures for the same languages, with the best system averaging 35.93% WER and no system falling below 24% on any language. Africa-targeted training, not model scale or nominal language coverage, best predicts performance.

evidence.snippet: Reading a code catalog beats ranking it: hit@5 0.843 vs 0.314, benchmark included.

reviewContext.abstract: whichfn Find the function you need by describing the situation you're in. Reading a code catalog beats ranking it: hit@5 0.843 vs 0.314, benchmark included. benchmark claude code-search developer-tools llm rag retrieval # whichfn **Find the function you need by describing the situation you're in.** ```bash whichfn ask "I need to know if this file changed since the last run" ``` You describe the **situation**. The docstring describes the **mechanism** — *"returns a stable digest of every tracked path plus its mtime and size."* They share no words, so grep has nothing to match and BM25 has nothing to score. That is not a tuning problem. There is no signal in the channel. `whichfn` builds a catalog of your public documented functions and puts **the whole thing** in front of a model, which reads it and picks. --- ## Why reading instead of retrieving I run a long-lived agent with a large Python codebase behind it, and it kept writing functions it already had. I assumed I needed a better retriever, so I built a benchmark to choose one. The benchmark said the retriever was never the problem. Measured on that codebase — 2,318 documented public functions, 51 questions: | | hit@1 | hit@3 | hit@5 | MRR | |---|---|---|---|---| | BM25 over the same catalog | 0.235 | 0.294 | 0.314 | 0.277 | | **Reading the catalog** | **0.725** | **0.824** | **0.843** | **0.776** | | Local dense embeddings *(see caveat)* | 0.000 | — | 0.020 | 0.010 | Paired per query; the BM25→read gap on hit@5 has a 5,000-sample bootstrap CI90 of **[+0.176, +0.412]**, which excludes zero. **Why lexical loses matters more than by how much.** Median Jaccard overlap between a question and its target's docstring: **0.029**. And BM25 doesn't miss narrowly — when it misses, the median rank of the right answer is **334 out of 2,318**. At rank 8 you have a ranking problem you could fix. At rank 334 there is nothing to rank. So the bottleneck is the **representation**. A docstring says what a function *is*; it never says what situation you'd be in when you need it. A reader can infer the second from the first. A term-matcher cannot. ## Install Not on PyPI. It is one file with one dependency: ```bash git clone https://github.com/massimiliano1991/whichfn pip install anthropic export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... python3 whichfn/whichfn.py ask "..." ``` Python 3.10+. ## Use ```bash whichfn ask "I keep double-charging people when the webhook retries" whichfn ask "..." --path src/ -k 5 --json whichfn ask "..." --exclude 'tests/*' --exclude 'migrations/*' whichfn catalog --stats # how big is my catalog, what does a question cost whichfn bench # measure ranking vs reading on YOUR code whichfn selftest # offline, no API key needed ``` **Run `catalog` first.** What you leave in decides everything downstream: ```console $ python3 whichfn.py catalog --path ~/src/myproject | wc -l 2603 ``` Vendored dependencies are pruned automatically — any directory holding a `*.dist-info` or `*.egg-info` is a pip target, not your code. On the repo this tool came from that one rule cut the catalog from 10,700 entries to 2,603. Use `--exclude` for the rest. ## Cost, and the real constraint Context is no longer the limit — a 1M-token window swallows every catalog I have measured. **Cost is the limit.** | codebase | functions | catalog | |---|---|---| | the repo this came from | 2,603 | 376 KB (≈94k tokens) | | CPython's own stdlib | 6,663 | 681 KB (≈170k tokens) | *(character counts measured; token figures are ≈chars/4, not counted — run `catalog --stats` for the exact number from the API.)* The catalog is sent as a **cached prefix**, so the first question in a session is a cache *write* — 1.25x base input, not 1.0x — and the rest pay about a tenth. At Opus prices a 94k-token catalog is roughly **$0.59 cold and $0.05 cached**; `--model claude-haiku-4-5` is a fifth of that. Cache TTL is 5 minutes — ask in bursts. `--budget` (default 150k tokens) is a **cost** guard, not a context guard. Past it, `whichfn` ranks with BM25 first, reads the top slice, and prints a warning saying it did. Ranking is the fallback, not the design. Note what that means for the second row of the table above: the stdlib catalog is over the default budget, so at factory settings `whichfn` pre-filters it instead of reading it whole. Raise `--budget` to read it all. The guard estimates tokens as `chars/3`, which over-counts on purpose: it is a spending limit, so it errs toward pre-filtering. `catalog --stats` reports the exact count from the API, which is lower — between roughly 450k and 600k characters the two disagree, and the guard is the one that decides. ## Check the numbers yourself `whichfn bench` reproduces the method on your code: 1. samples N documented functions at a fixed seed; 2. a **blind** annotator — it sees only name, signature and docstring, never the retrievers or the point of the exercise — writes the situation each one solves; 3. any question containing the target's name, a ≥4-character piece of it, or its module name is **discarded, not repaired**; 4. both arms are scored against the same catalog and written to `whichfn-bench.json`, every question and both ranks, so you can read the failures. ### The bias in it, stated plainly The questions are generated **from docstrings**, so a method that reads docstrings is being scored on a paraphrase of its own input. A human asking from real ignorance is a harder test than this. I don't think it accounts for a 0.53 gap, but it inflates it, and you should assume the true margin is smaller than the table. That's the reason the benchmark ships instead of just the number. On four questions I wrote myself before running anything, three returned the right function at #1 and one missed completely — small n, reported because it cuts against me. ### The dense-embedding caveat — read before quoting the 0.020 That row is **one** setup: Qwen-1.5B, raw mean-pooled hidden states, run locally. reviewContext.abstract: voice-benchmark Open-source, fully automated benchmarks for realtime speech AI — streaming STT (WER, finalize latency, TTFT, cost) and end-to-end voice-agent pipelines # voice-benchmark Open-source, fully automated benchmarks for realtime speech AI — from streaming STT alone to complete STT → LLM → TTS agent loops. Inspired by [benchmarks.speko.ai](https://benchmarks.speko.ai/). Every number on the leaderboard is produced end-to-end by CI: a GitHub Actions run executes the harness against real vendor endpoints, writes versioned JSON results, regenerates markdown tables and a static leaderboard site, and publishes them via GitHub Pages. No hand-edited numbers. ## What we measure ### Realtime STT track | Metric | Definition | | --- | --- | | **WER** | Word error rate of finalized transcripts vs reference (Sclite-style scoring, jiwer) | | **Finalize latency** | Time from caller silence to finalized transcript — p50 / p90 | | **Time to first token (TTFT)** | Time from audio start to first transcript token — p50 / p90 | | **Cost** | Vendor's published streaming rate per 1k minutes | ### Voice-agent E2E track Full loop latency: user stops speaking → agent audio starts playing back. Decomposed into STT finalize + LLM first token + TTS time-to-first-audio. ## Vendors Realtime STT: AssemblyAI · ElevenLabs Scribe v2 Realtime · Deepgram Nova-3 / Flux · OpenAI GPT-4o Transcribe (realtime) · Soniox · Cartesia Ink-2 · Google Chirp 3 · Gladia · Inworld · Smallest AI Pulse · xAI Grok STT · Alibaba Qwen3-ASR E2E: any combination of an STT adapter, an LLM (Anthropic / OpenAI), and a TTS adapter. ## Quickstart ```bash pip install -e ".[dev]" cp .env.example .env.local && set -a; source .env.local; set +a # paste vendor keys # run every enabled provider on the default dataset voicebench run --track stt --all # one provider voicebench run --track stt --provider deepgram-nova-3 # E2E loop benchmark voicebench run --track e2e --stt deepgram-nova-3 --llm claude-sonnet --tts elevenlabs # regenerate leaderboard + site from stored results voicebench report ``` TypeScript SDK: ```bash npm install npx tsx src/ts/run.ts --track stt --provider soniox-stt-rt-v5 ``` ## Repository layout ``` datasets/ manifest + audio + references (see datasets/README.md) providers/ one adapter per vendor — implement BaseProvider to add yours src/voicebench/ Python harness: runner, metrics, timing, reporting, CLI src/ts/ TypeScript SDK mirroring the Python adapters results/ committed JSON per run (versioned, append-only) site/ leaderboard generator -> GitHub Pages output .github/workflows/ nightly + manual benchmark runs; auto-publishes the site CONTRIBUTING.md how to add a provider or dataset docs/METHODOLOGY.md scoring definitions, normalization rules, caveats ``` ## Methodology See [docs/METHODOLOGY.md](docs/METHODOLOGY.md). Short version: 1. Fixed, versioned audio fixtures with human-verified references. 2. Streaming over each vendor's realtime websocket with realistic chunking (20–100 ms frames), timestamps recorded client-side at send/receive. 3. Finalized text normalized identically for hypothesis and reference before WER. 4. Latency percentiles computed over all turns; runs are re-executed nightly so numbers reflect current vendor behaviour, not a one-time snapshot. ## Adding a provider Implement `BaseProvider` (`connect`, `stream_audio`, `finalize`, `close`) and a small YAML descriptor; see `providers/README.md` and any existing adapter. The runner, metrics, and leaderboard pick it up automatically. ## License MIT — see [LICENSE](LICENSE).

reviewContext.abstract: LLMs are increasingly used to analyze spreadsheets, CSV files, and other structured data, but producing a correct-looking answer is not the same as producing a trustworthy analysis. A trustworthy result should be supported by a valid path from the user question to the relevant data evidence. This requirement creates two diagnostic questions: whether an LLM can refuse to answer or ask for clarification when such a path does not exist, and whether it can preserve the correct analysis when the same evidence is expressed in different table forms. We introduce TrustDABench, a benchmark that operationalizes these questions as reliability and robustness. Starting from the evidence-path view, we derive 19 perturbation operators and instantiate them through an Agentic-LLM-based generation framework. TrustDABench contains 2,340 human-verified perturbed instances, and we evaluate eight representative LLMs. The results show substantial headroom: the best reliability result is only 24.21% average MRS, achieved by GPT-5.5, while the best robustness result still has 9.10% average ASR, achieved by Claude-Sonnet-5. The failures are systematic: models rarely detect conflicting evidence, often continue along executable but unsupported analysis paths, and remain sensitive to perturbations that change observation boundaries or cross-table relations. These findings suggest that stronger evidence-boundary recognition and representation-invariant reasoning are still needed for reliable structured-data analysis.

reviewContext.abstract: teamily-private-benchmark Tooling for building and scoring a private agent benchmark from real product traffic. Questions deliberately not included. # teamily-private-benchmark Tooling for building and scoring a **private** agent benchmark from real product traffic. This repository holds the *machinery* — the selection, labelling, rubric-generation and scoring code — and deliberately holds **no questions**. The questions are verbatim customer prompts. They stay out of git for two independent reasons, and either one alone would be sufficient: 1. They contain real business content — supplier strategies, open trading positions, product roadmaps, named clinics. 2. A benchmark whose questions are public stops measuring anything, because vendors can train against it. `.gitignore` blocks `*.jsonl`, `*.csv` and `_cache*/` at the root so a stray `git add -A` cannot leak a question set. ## The pipeline ``` production traffic │ ▼ build_pool.py filter labelled traffic down to benchmark-eligible prompts │ ▼ select_questions.py largest-remainder quotas + greedy multi-objective pick │ (quality + sector deficit + language deficit − user reuse) ▼ scrub_pii.py three layers: regex → LLM for names → verification re-scan │ ├──► gen_items.py per-question checklist (the rubric) ├──► label_difficulty.py easy | medium | hard └──► label_spec_quality.py well_specified | workable | underspecified │ ▼ make_review_sheet.py export → human review → apply ``` ## Scoring `docs/Scoring_Framework.md` is the specification. In short: three tiers — **Gate** (did anything get delivered at all), **Core** (the substance), **Decor** (polish) — merged with WorkBuddy Bench's fixed-penalty judge: ``` S = 0 if any Gate item fails S = max(0, 1 − Σ penalty(failed items)) otherwise ``` Penalties are `major 0.3 / normal 0.2 / minor 0.1`. The penalty mass `M = Σ penalty` over non-fatal items is deliberately greater than 1, so the tolerance `τ = 1/M` is the share of mass a deliverable may fail before scoring zero. **`M` excludes Gate items** — they are pass/fail on their own axis and including them would compute a tolerance that no deliverable is graded against. ## Design notes that are easy to get wrong - **The tier is computed, never reported by the model.** In both labellers the LLM scores countable axes and code reads the tier off them. Asked directly for a verdict, the model put 81% of the set in one bucket; the same axes, combined arithmetically, give a usable 21/53/25. - **Score-affecting values reject rather than coerce.** A silently corrected severity appears in a distribution as if it had been measured. - **The output is rebuilt from the cache, not from the run.** An interrupted run must never overwrite a complete file with a partial one. - **Every rubric item must quote its prompt.** The cited span is the whole basis for "this requirement is the user's, not the model's". The normaliser lives in exactly one place (`gen_items._span`) and the review sheet imports it, so the sheet cannot grade by a rule the generator did not enforce. - **Bindings are on `prompt_sha256`, never `qid`.** A qid is a position in one selection and moves the moment the set is re-selected. ## Working in this repository The question set lives OUTSIDE the working tree and is reached through a gitignored symlink, so there is exactly one copy of the customer prompts and it is not inside a public repo: ```bash git clone https://github.com/xintong-tensoropera/teamily-private-benchmark.git cd teamily-private-benchmark ln -s /path/to/your/questions data # gitignored; script defaults point at data/ ln -s /path/to/your/.env .env # OPENROUTER_API_KEY git config core.hooksPath .githooks # REQUIRED — see below ``` `.githooks/pre-commit` blocks a commit that would publish questions. It checks what is actually STAGED, in three ways: data file extensions, paths under `data/`, and — the one that matters — whether any staged text quotes the question set verbatim. That last check catches a README or docstring that pasted a customer prompt in, which is how two leaks nearly shipped in the first commit here. Hooks are not cloned with a repository, so the `core.hooksPath` line above is not optional. Note `.gitignore` lists both `data` and `data/`. A trailing slash matches directories only, and git treats a symlink as a file, so `data/` alone does not ignore a `data -> ...` symlink. ```bash uv run --with pyyaml python scripts/gen_items.py \ --questions data/questions.jsonl \ --out data/items.jsonl --cache-dir data/_cache --workers 8 ``` All labelling scripts are content-addressed and concurrent: reruns hit cache, cost nothing, and are safe to interrupt. ## The examples in `configs/checklist_schema_v2.yaml` are synthetic The few-shot examples that teach the generator were rewritten from invented prompts. They preserve every lesson — specs become one item per number, a numbered content list is not N specs, an exclusion list is a rule anchor, severity discipline — without reproducing any customer's request.

reviewContext.abstract: spanish-hate-speech-benchmark Spanish hate speech detection benchmark using classical machine learning, BETO fine-tuning, and prompt-based baselines for binary and target classification. # Detección del Discurso de Odio en Español Repositorio del TFG orientado a la clasificación de discurso de odio en español. El proyecto combina dos tareas principales: - Clasificación binaria de odio/no odio sobre el corpus de Twitter. - Identificación de categoría objetivo sobre HateCheck-es. El trabajo compara varios enfoques: baseline con TF-IDF + regresión logística, BETO fine-tuned, BETO congelado con embeddings, zero-shot, few-shot y variantes con preprocesamiento distinto. Los resultados, matrices de confusión y figuras para la memoria se generan en `RESULTS/`. ## Estructura - `BASELINE/`: entrenamiento de modelos clásicos y traductor leet-speak. - `FINE-TUNNING/`: preparación de datos, fine-tuning de BETO, evaluación y análisis. - `scripts/`: utilidades para ejecutar experimentos, comparar modelos y generar figuras. - `DATASETS/`: corpora fuente y versiones limpias. - `DOCUMENTACION/`: material de presentación del TFG. ## Requisitos Entorno recomendado: Python 3.10 o superior. Instalación: ```bash pip install -r requirements.txt ``` Algunas evaluaciones requieren además credenciales o modelos externos: - `scripts/run_groq_binary.py` necesita la variable de entorno `GROQ_API_KEY`. - Los scripts de Hugging Face descargan modelos como `dccuchile/bert-base-spanish-wwm-uncased` y `MoritzLaurer/mDeBERTa-v3-base-mnli-xnli`. ## Flujo de trabajo 1. Preparar datos con `FINE-TUNNING/preparar_datos.py`. 2. Entrenar o reutilizar los baselines en `BASELINE/`. 3. Entrenar BETO con `FINE-TUNNING/entrenamiento_beto.py` y `FINE-TUNNING/entrenamiento_targets.py`. 4. Evaluar con `FINE-TUNNING/evaluacion_beto.py`, `FINE-TUNNING/evaluacion_targets.py` o `scripts/run_all_evaluations.py`. 5. Generar figuras con `scripts/generate_thesis_figures.py`. ## Datasets y resultados Los CSV de `DATASETS/` son la base original del trabajo. Los archivos dentro de `FINE-TUNNING/` y `RESULTS/` se consideran derivados y se excluyen del control de versiones para evitar subir artefactos pesados o regenerables. ## Notas - El repositorio conserva el código y los datasets fuente necesarios para reproducir el trabajo. - Los modelos entrenados y las salidas experimentales se regeneran ejecutando los scripts correspondientes. - Si quieres publicar una versión aún más limpia, el siguiente paso razonable es agrupar los scripts en un paquete Python con `src/` y añadir un `LICENSE`.

reviewContext.abstract: Recent advances in single-image 3D Gaussian head reconstruction have enabled highly realistic and freely renderable digital heads from a single portrait. However, reconstruction and rendering can weaken the forgery traces in the source portrait, making the resulting 3D face difficult to classify whether its underlying face is real or fake, and thereby posing risks to identity authentication and face privacy. To study this problem, we introduce the first large-scale benchmark for this task by collecting real portraits and fake portraits from multiple sources and evaluate representative existing detectors on this benchmark, revealing their lack of explicit mechanisms for retaining fine-grained information and maintaining feature consistency across rendered views. To directly address these two limitations, we propose a detector trained with a two-stage strategy. In Stage I, masked autoencoding encourages the visual backbone to retain the fine-grained appearance information required for local reconstruction, while multi-view contrastive learning enforces feature consistency across rendered views of the same head. Since CLS tokens at different depths exhibit complementary spatial attention patterns, Stage II freezes the adapted backbone and concatenates low-, middle-, and high-level CLS tokens for classification. Experiments show that our method achieves the highest accuracy and ranks first across all reported metrics among the evaluated detectors.

reviewContext.abstract: Reliable underwater perception requires complementary sensing under variable visibility. Optical cameras capture appearance and semantics but degrade rapidly with turbidity, whereas imaging sonar preserves geometry while exhibiting distinct range-azimuth structure and acoustic artifacts. Existing MLLMs, built primarily on optical encoders, are therefore ill-suited to model sonar or adaptively exploit sonar-optical complementarity. We propose SonarLLM, a sonar-optical MLLM that treats sonar as a native perceptual modality. It combines a sonar-specific encoder, modality-specific physics-aware feature enhancement, and reliability-aware hierarchical fusion to align acoustic structure with optical semantics and dynamically adjust their contributions as sensing quality changes. We also introduce SonarBench, a paired benchmark that spans four tasks: recognition, counting, visual question answering, and captioning; and, across the benchmark, three input settings: sonar-only, optical-only, and fusion. By fixing the scene and sonar observation while varying optical degradation, SonarBench enables controlled measurement of cross-modal complementarity. SonarLLM achieves 72.0% macro accuracy across sonar-only recognition, counting, and VQA, outperforming the strongest baseline by 34.4 percentage points, and 68.7% under fusion, exceeding the best baseline by 25.1 points. For recognition and counting, the fusion-over-optical gain grows from 6.0 to 36.0 points as turbidity increases, indicating the increasing complementary value of sonar under controlled optical degradation. Together, these results show that robust heterogeneous perception depends not only on adding sonar, but on representing and weighting it according to its sensing characteristics.

reviewContext.abstract: Modern text-to-image (T2I) models often have similar total scores but different strengths, making practical selection difficult. Fine-grained benchmarks decompose prompts into questions, yet often return them to prompt scores and fixed categories, weakening attribution and ignoring complexity. Related requirements are also scored separately or as one total, obscuring basic versus compositional failure. We present QC-T2I-Bench, a question-centric framework that converts open prompts into attributed atomic questions and organizes their dependencies with Davidsonian Scene Graphs (DSGs). We use hierarchy-constrained question aggregation to exclude downstream questions after a prerequisite fails and to prevent simple and complex prompts from receiving the same total weight. We then use the DSG structure to measure joint success within prompts and compare repeated entities across prompts, separating basic realization failures from failures under additional requirements. We evaluate multiple open-source T2I models on English and Chinese prompts. The resulting question-level evidence supports reliable ranking and fine-grained diagnosis: joint completion falls from 80.7\% for components with two capabilities to 37.2\% for those with seven or more. Finally, we reuse the same records for training-free routing; our cost-aware router matches ERNIE's 89.51-point estimate with 21.3\% less GPU-s/MP.

reviewContext.abstract: rlvr-generalization Does RLVR teach reasoning or teach the benchmark? GRPO post-training on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B in pure PyTorch, evaluated across math, science, and medical reasoning. generalization grpo llm machine-learning-research post-training pytorch reasoning reinforcement-learning rlvr # Does RLVR Teach Reasoning — or Teach the Benchmark? **Reproducing RLVR post-training on `Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B` in pure PyTorch, then stress-testing whether the reasoning gains survive a domain shift.** [![Python 3.10+](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.10%2B-blue.svg)](https://www.python.org/) [![PyTorch](https://img.shields.io/badge/PyTorch-2.4%2B-ee4c2c.svg)](https://pytorch.org/) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](LICENSE) [![CI](https://github.com/SaifSyed08/rlvr-generalization/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/SaifSyed08/rlvr-generalization/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Status: active](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-active%20research-brightgreen.svg)](#roadmap) *Independent research · Austin, TX · started July 2026* --- ## The question Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) reliably moves math benchmarks. `Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B` post-trained with GRPO on GSM8K/MATH climbs several points on held-out math evals, and the field reads that as *"the model learned to reason."* That reading assumes something nobody checks by default: **that the improvement is a property of the policy, not of the benchmark.** This repo makes that assumption falsifiable. One training run, three evaluation domains: ``` ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B (base) │ └───────────────┬──────────────┘ │ GRPO · verifiable reward · math-only prompts │ ┌───────────────▼──────────────┐ │ Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B (RLVR) │ └───────────────┬──────────────┘ │ ┌───────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ┌───────────────┐ ┌───────────────┐ ┌───────────────┐ │ IN-DOMAIN │ │ NEAR-DOMAIN │ │ FAR-DOMAIN │ │ math │ │ science │ │ medical │ ├───────────────┤ ├───────────────┤ ├───────────────┤ │ GSM8K │ │ GPQA-Diamond │ │ MedQA (USMLE) │ │ MATH-500 │ │ MMLU-STEM │ │ MedMCQA │ │ AIME 2024/25 │ │ SciQ │ │ PubMedQA │ └───────────────┘ └───────────────┘ └───────────────┘ expected up ??? ??? ``` **H0 (benchmark-specific):** gains concentrate in-domain and decay monotonically with distance from the training distribution. **H1 (broad generalization):** gains persist across all three domains, tracking format compliance and chain length rather than topic. Both outcomes are publishable results. This repo is built so the answer isn't a matter of taste — every number ships with its seed, its decode config, and its per-item generations. --- ## Why this design is not the obvious one Three choices that most RLVR reproductions get wrong, and what this repo does instead: | Failure mode | What usually happens | What this repo does | |---|---|---| | **Format confound** | RLVR teaches `\boxed{}` compliance. The parser then finds answers it previously missed, and that shows up as "reasoning gains." | Every eval reports **two** accuracies: strict-parse and permissive-parse. If the gap closes post-training, the gain was formatting. See [`docs/methodology.md`](docs/methodology.md). | | **Contamination** | AIME/GSM8K leakage into the base model is quietly assumed away. | N-gram overlap scan between train prompts and every eval set, reported in [`docs/reproducibility.md`](docs/reproducibility.md). | | **Single-seed claims** | One run, one seed, 2-point delta, declared victory. | 3 seeds minimum; deltas ship with bootstrap CIs. Anything inside the CI is reported as null, not spun. | The last one matters most. A 1.5B model on AIME has ~30 items — the noise floor is enormous, and a lot of published deltas live inside it. --- ## Method **Algorithm:** GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) — critic-free, group-normalized advantages. Chosen over PPO because a 1.5B policy plus a 1.5B value head does not fit the compute budget, and because the reward is a scalar verifier with no dense signal for a critic to fit. For a prompt `q`, sample a group of `G` completions. The advantage for completion `i` is its reward, normalized within the group: ``` A_i = (r_i − mean(r_1..r_G)) / (std(r_1..r_G) + eps) ``` No value network. No reward model. The reward is a **verifier**: | Component | Weight | Signal | |---|---|---| | Answer correctness | `1.0` | SymPy-normalized equivalence against ground truth | | Format compliance | `0.2` | well-formed ` ... ` + `\boxed{}` | | Length penalty | `−0.05` | soft penalty past the token budget, kills degenerate rambling | Correctness is deliberately the dominant term. Format reward is small on purpose — large format weights are exactly how you manufacture the confound in row 1 of the table above. **Full hyperparameters and their justification:** [`configs/grpo_qwen2.5_math_1.5b.yaml`](configs/grpo_qwen2.5_math_1.5b.yaml) --- ## Results > **Status: training runs in progress.** This table is the pre-registered output shape, not results. > Numbers land here as runs finish; nothing is reported before 3 seeds complete. > Pre-registration matters — it's what makes the null result reportable instead of quietly dropped. | Domain | Benchmark | Base | RLVR | Δ | 95% CI | |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---| | Math (in) | GSM8K | — | — | — | — | | Math (in) | MATH-500 | — | — | — | — | | Math (in) | AIME 2024 | — | — | — | — | | Science (near) | GPQA-Diamond | — | — | — | — | | Science (near) | MMLU-STEM | — | — | — | — | | Medical (far) | MedQA (USMLE) | — | — | — | — | | Medical (far) | MedMCQA | — | — | — | — | | Medical (far) | PubMedQA | — | — | — | — | **Diagnostics tracked alongside accuracy** — these are what actually distinguish H0 from H1: - `strict − permissive` parse gap, per domain (formatting confound) - mean chain-of-thought length, base vs. RLVR (verbosity confound) - pass@1 vs. pass@8 (did the policy sharpen, or did it acquire capability?) - per-domain

reviewContext.abstract: Clinical decision-making often involves prioritizing ethical values, such as beneficence, non-maleficence, respecting a patient's autonomy, and justice. Recent work has begun to assess how large language models (LLMs) make such subjective, value-laden clinical judgments. However, evaluations of LLM decision-making in rare disease care contexts, where ethical tensions are ubiquitous and where scarce prior information likely impacts LLM behavior, are still lacking. Here, we present a benchmark of 208 clinically grounded rare disease vignettes, each of which presents genuine, high-stakes conflicts. When prompting 11 state-of-the-art LLMs to choose between clinically defensible yet ethically conflicting next steps embedded within these vignettes, we found that all evaluated models consistently prioritized justice over other core bioethical principles. Specifically, models overwhelmingly favor equal resource allocation over need-based considerations, indicating LLMs' limited responsiveness to differences in clinical severity or situational context. We also identify a strong authority-framing effect: models favor justice in committee-based contexts and shift toward beneficence and autonomy only when final decisions are framed as being made by clinicians or patients respectively. Our work suggests that institutional pressures surrounding rare disease resource utilization may be silently reflected in LLM-based decision support systems, with finer ethical considerations disregarded.

reviewContext.abstract: Automated high-density storage systems (warehouses, robotic parking, plant logistics, etc.) require fleets of agents to move through scarce task-critical resources and then park without obstructing future operations. We introduce Pivot-and-Station Multi-Agent Path Finding (PS-MAPF), a MAPF variant in which a subset of tasked agents must each visit one of a set of interchangeable pivots (e.g., workstations) before the entire fleet terminates at anonymous stations, one agent per station. We characterize solvability completely: every instance on a 2-edge-connected graph is solvable, and, on arbitrary connected graphs, a structural effective-distance measure relative to the number of unoccupied vertices gives a necessary and sufficient condition. We prove that minimizing station-makespan or station-flowtime is NP-hard already with a single pivot. We present three algorithms, a complete baseline, a SAT-based optimal solver, and Pivot-Prioritized Planning (PPP), the last solving 74-89% of benchmark instances with makespan and flowtime orders of magnitude below the baseline.

reviewContext.abstract: odinbench A small cross-model benchmark for OpenAI-compatible APIs and Ollama benchmark evals llm ollama # OdinBench OdinBench is a small, dependency-free harness for comparing language models on the tasks you actually care about. It runs the same prompt corpus against OpenAI-compatible APIs or local Ollama models, grades every answer against an all-pass rubric, and writes JSON plus a readable Markdown report. The included corpus is intentionally small. Replace it with your own tasks before treating the scores as meaningful. ## Quick start Python 3.9 or newer is enough. Run a local Ollama model and use another local model as the judge: ```bash python3 odinbench.py \ --models ollama:qwen3:8b,ollama:gemma3:12b \ --judge ollama:qwen3:8b ``` Run models from an OpenAI-compatible API: ```bash export OPENAI_API_KEY="your-key" python3 odinbench.py \ --models openai:gpt-4.1-mini,openai:gpt-4.1 \ --judge openai:gpt-4.1 ``` Set `OPENAI_BASE_URL` to use another provider that implements the Chat Completions API. Reports are written to `reports/`. Generated reports are ignored by Git because model output may contain prompt data. ## Model syntax Every model uses `provider:model` syntax: - `ollama:qwen3:8b` calls the local Ollama API at `127.0.0.1:11434`. - `openai:gpt-4.1` calls `$OPENAI_BASE_URL/chat/completions` with `$OPENAI_API_KEY`. OdinBench sends prompts and candidate outputs to the judge model. If the corpus contains private data, use a judge you trust or keep judging local. ## Add tasks Edit `tasks.json`. Each task needs an ID, category, prompt, and rubric: ```json { "id": "strict_json", "category": "format", "prompt": "Return the supplied fields as JSON and nothing else.", "rubric": [ "Output parses as JSON", "Contains every required field", "Contains no prose or Markdown fences" ] } ``` Rubrics are all-pass. One failed criterion fails the task. ## Limits An LLM judge is useful, but it is not ground truth. Keep deterministic checks in the rubric, inspect failures, and use repeated runs when model variance matters. Latency also includes local network and provider overhead, so compare runs made under similar conditions. ## Test ```bash python3 -m unittest -v ``` ## License MIT

reviewContext.abstract: NPU-vs-CPU-LLM-Inference-Benchmark Benchmarking LLM inference on an Intel Core Ultra 5 225F's built-in NPU (13 TOPS INT8, OpenVINO GenAI) versus its CPU, to determine when — if ever — NPU offload is worth it for local LLM inference on consumer edge hardware. benchmarking llm npu openvino # NPU vs. CPU LLM Inference Benchmark Benchmarking LLM inference on an Intel Core Ultra 5 225F's built-in NPU (13 TOPS INT8, OpenVINO GenAI) versus its CPU, to determine when — if ever — NPU offload is worth it for local LLM inference on consumer edge hardware. ## Conclusion **On this hardware, the NPU is not a speed feature — it's only really useful when the CPU is under load.** At idle, the CPU wins outright: it beats the NPU on both TTFT and TPOT, at every model size and prompt length tested (H1, confirmed). The NPU's TTFT is dominated by a large, roughly-fixed cost — likely its static-shape compilation requirement — that barely moves whether the prompt is 33 tokens or 352 (H4: partially confirmed — true for prefill, not for decode, which does narrow somewhat at the larger 3B model size). The result that actually matters: under CPU contention, the picture flips. When background CPU load rises from 0% to 75%, CPU inference throughput degrades 65-67% — but NPU throughput degrades only 9-13% (H3, confirmed, the strongest and cleanest result in the project). The NPU doesn't win by being fast; it wins by being unbothered. That makes it the right choice specifically for background or concurrent inference — running alongside other CPU-heavy work — not for a one-off "fastest single response" use case, where the CPU remains the better pick on this particular 13-TOPS part. ## Resume framing > Built a reproducible benchmark harness comparing NPU vs. CPU LLM inference on an > Intel Core Ultra 5 225F (OpenVINO GenAI, INT4-symmetric quantization); measured > throughput and latency across model sizes, prompt lengths, and CPU contention > levels to determine when NPU offload is worth it on consumer edge hardware. ## Hypotheses - **H1:** CPU wins raw decode throughput, because token generation is memory-bandwidth-bound and the NPU shares the same DDR5 bus as the CPU. - **H3:** NPU wins under CPU contention — inference on the NPU degrades far less when the CPU is busy with other work, and vice versa. - **H4:** Prefill and decode behave differently — prefill is compute-bound (the NPU's supposed strength), decode isn't. *(H2, an energy-per-token hypothesis, was dropped — Windows lacks a simple RAPL path, and the two real options — a wall meter or Intel PCM's driver — weren't worth the added scope for this project.)* ## Setup - Hardware: Intel Core Ultra 5 225F (no iGPU), Windows, native (not WSL2/VM — the NPU isn't exposed through virtualization or WSL2 as of this writing). - Model: `Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct`, exported to OpenVINO IR with `optimum-cli export openvino --weight-format int4 --sym --ratio 1.0 --group-size 128`. - Toolkit: OpenVINO GenAI, via `openvino_genai.LLMPipeline`. - Metrics: `PerfMetrics.get_load_time()`, `get_ttft()`, `get_tpot()`, plus raw per-call values pooled across runs (not averaged-per-run) for TTFT and TPOT, using `raw_metrics.m_times_to_first_token` and `raw_metrics.m_new_token_times`. - Method: one warm-up call per device (excluded from stats), then 4 measured runs across 5 varied prompts, each generating 50 tokens. ## First results Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, 5 prompts, 4 measured runs per device: | Metric | NPU | CPU | |---|---|---| | Load time | 1872 ms | 1170 ms | | TTFT (mean, std) | 1874.73, 7.48 ms | 102.28, 13.19 ms | | TPOT (mean, std) | 52.10, 1.26 ms | 20.42, 3.95 ms | **CPU won every metric measured so far**, including TTFT — which H4 predicted would favor the NPU, since prefill is supposedly the NPU's strength. It didn't. NPU's TTFT std is small relative to its mean (consistently slow, not erratically slow). CPU's TPOT std is proportionally noisier relative to its mean than NPU's. ## Model-size comparison (1.5B vs. 3B) | | 1.5B NPU | 3B NPU | 1.5B CPU | 3B CPU | |---|---|---|---|---| | TTFT | ~1875ms | ~2886ms | ~90ms | ~160ms | | TPOT | ~52.3ms | ~62.6ms | ~18.5ms | ~31.7ms | NPU/CPU ratio: TTFT ~19.7x (1.5B) vs ~18x (3B) — barely moved. TPOT ~2.83x (1.5B) vs ~1.97x (3B) — meaningfully narrowed. **Mixed result on the "model too small" theory.** Holds for TPOT/decode (NPU becomes relatively more competitive as model size grows, as predicted) but not for TTFT/prefill (ratio barely changed) — suggesting TTFT and TPOT are bottlenecked by different things on this hardware. ## Prompt-length scaling One fixed topic, four lengths (~33/71/181/352 input tokens), repeated 3x each with shuffled order to separate real effects from position or noise. **NPU TTFT is essentially flat regardless of prompt length** (~2900-2990ms across the whole range, on both the 1.5B and 3B models) — consistent with a large, dominant fixed cost (likely the NPU's static-shape compilation requirement) that doesn't scale with actual prefill work in this range. **CPU TTFT scales with length, but non-monotonically at the short end.** Confirmed via order-shuffle that the shortest (33-token) prompt reproducibly has *higher* CPU TTFT than the next-shortest (71-token) prompt, regardless of which loop position each one lands in — a genuine property of the prompt length, not a positional artifact. At the long end, CPU TTFT scaling looked super-linear in early single-run testing; more repeats needed to confirm the exact shape now that a measurement bug (below) has been fixed. **Methodology note — repeated-run caching bug, found and fixed.** Reusing identical prompt text across repeats triggered OpenVINO's stateful KV-cache reuse (meant for real multi-turn chat), which skipped most of the prefill on repeat runs and produced artificially fast (and invalid) TTFT numbers. Fixed by appending a unique per-repeat marker to each prompt so no two calls ever share identical text — confirmed the anomaly disappeared after the fix. ## CP

reviewContext.abstract: loop-engineering-benchmark A reproducible benchmark comparing single-prompt and loop-engineered AI agents on autonomous software bug repair. ai-agents autonomous-agents benchmark llm software-engineering # Loop Engineering vs Normal Prompting Benchmark A reproducible, observable autonomous bug-repair laboratory for measuring when iterative coding agents are worth their extra inference cost. This is not an LLM demo. It is an experimental platform with a clean FastAPI commerce target, twenty controlled defects, four primary agent architectures, an adaptive agent, isolated Git worktrees, persistent loop state, hidden evaluation, SQLite telemetry, result exports, charts, and a Streamlit explorer. ## The comparison Normal prompting is a single transition: ```text Issue → context → model → patch → tests → stop ``` Loop engineering is a controlled state machine: ```text Goal → observe → diagnose → plan → act → verify → reflect → remember → decide → repeat/stop ``` It is more than retrying. The loop selects context, records explicit hypotheses and plans, uses objective test feedback, persists state outside model context, detects repeated failures, changes strategy, enforces budgets, and may require independent reviewer approval. The primary architectures are: | Architecture | Attempts | Feedback | Explicit stages | Persistent state | Reviewer | |---|---:|---|---|---|---| | `single` | 1 | No | No | Result only | No | | `basic-loop` | ≤5 | Test output | No | Yes | No | | `structured-loop` | ≤5 | Test + reflection | Yes | Yes | No | | `evaluator-loop` | ≤5 | Test + reflection | Yes | Yes | Independent | `adaptive-loop` starts cheaply and escalates only after failure. The completed 240-run reference experiment and its correction policy are summarized in [benchmark results](docs/RESULTS.md). All architectures share the same response-protocol adapter. It accepts common unified-diff field names and raw fenced diffs, normalizes malformed hunk counts, accepts patches without trailing context, recognizes already-applied patches, and permits at most one format-only retry (`model.format_retries`) when a diff is missing or Git rejects its syntax/context. The retry is grounded in current source, receives no test feedback, and may not reconsider the solution, so it repairs serialization rather than adding a bug-fixing iteration. Its calls, tokens, cost, and latency are still included in the run metrics. ## Quick start Python 3.12+ and Git are required. ```bash python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate pip install -e '.[dev]' python -m pytest python benchmark.py --list-tasks ``` The default deterministic provider runs fully offline and intentionally produces no repair. It validates isolation, looping, persistence, logging, evaluation, and exports; do not interpret its scores as research results. For an OpenAI-compatible model, change `model.provider` to `openai-compatible`, set model pricing in `config.yaml`, and copy `.env.example` to `.env`. The CLI loads `.env` automatically: ```env LLM_API_KEY="your-private-key" LLM_BASE_URL="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1" LLM_MODEL="deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash" ``` ## Run experiments ```bash # One architecture and task python benchmark.py --agent structured-loop --task BUG-011 --runs 1 # Four primary architectures, all tasks, three repetitions (240 runs) python benchmark.py --agent all --runs 3 # Skills ablation python benchmark.py --agent structured-loop --runs 3 --without-skills # Preserve a failed worktree so the run can be resumed python benchmark.py --agent structured-loop --task BUG-011 --runs 1 --keep-worktrees python benchmark.py --resume BUG-011-structured-loop-R1- # Re-export an experiment or all stored results python benchmark.py --analyze --experiment-id EXP-... python benchmark.py --analyze ``` `python run_benchmark.py --scheduled` is scheduler-compatible; a cron or external scheduler can invoke it without manual prompting. The flag uses the same deterministic run queue and database. ## Fairness and success definition Every run starts from the same clean Git commit in its own worktree. The task mutation is committed before timing begins, so the agent begins with a clean faulty repository. Model, temperature, issue, visible tests, and tools remain fixed across architectures. Agent tools cannot access `benchmark/hidden_tests`. A task succeeds only when: 1. Its targeted visible tests pass. 2. The complete visible and system regression suite passes. 3. Its hidden evaluator tests pass. 4. For `evaluator-loop`, the independent reviewer approves. The application regression gate runs `tests/visible` and `tests/system` while excluding `tests/system/test_benchmark_platform.py`. That excluded file validates benchmark construction (catalog anchors, security boundaries, configuration, and protocol mechanics) and must not reject a behaviorally correct repair merely because its formatting differs from the clean fixture. The evaluator reviewer receives the issue, complete working-tree diff, post-patch contents of all modified source files and their bounded transitive local-import dependencies, and test output. Reviewer rejections replace the next iteration's feedback, so the developer responds to the critique rather than blindly reapplying the same patch. Failure, budget exhaustion, a hidden-test failure, regression, or an unanswerable clarification sets `human_intervention_required=true`. Budget gates are checked before accepting a test or review success, so a repair completed over its configured token, cost, or runtime limit is recorded as a budget failure while its objective test evidence remains auditable. ## Observability and outputs Each action is emitted as JSONL under `logs/`; complete model responses are retained in `logs/ .responses.jsonl`, and resumable state lives under `memory/`.
